name: Rational Inattention
description: People cannot process all available information, so they choose what to attend to by weighing the cost of attention against its payoff. Ignoring information can be a sensible choice, not just a lapse.
design_relevance_note: Explains why users skip information that is not worth the effort of reading; design should put information where its value to the user exceeds the effort of noticing it.
myth_risk_note: A theory with real experimental support for its core; the assumptions used in applied models are not all supported.
prevalence_note: Mainly an economics and macro-finance concept; Nielsen's article is a rare design-world citation.

findings.description: In laboratory experiments, subjects adjusted their attention in response to changes in incentives, as rational inattention models predict, but their behaviour was qualitatively inconsistent with information costs that are linear in Shannon entropy (a common assumption in applied work); a more flexible generalisation of the Shannon model fit best.

Rational inattention theory assumes agents cannot process all available information but choose which information to attend to; the review argues this yields behaviour with numerous empirically supported departures from standard models and a generally applicable framework combining human limitations with neoclassical optimisation.
